speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: A. V. ROE COMPANY STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH COMPANY OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Prime Minister, who is indoors today with a cold, I should like to report to the house on the discussions which have been proceeding in recent days between the government and senior officials of A. V. Roe Canada Limited. These discussions had as their aim the continuance of the plants of Avro Aircraft Limited and Orenda Engines Limited, and the companies' special design, research and production facilities.
The companies are at present engaged in the performance of certain contracts for the government apart from the discontinued Arrow program. Work on these other contracts will, of course, be continued. In addition, various new programs and extensions of existing programs have now been proposed by the companies to the government in the fields of military and civil aviation and nuclear power. These proposals have been carefully examined, and certain of them will be further studied in the hope that they will offer opportunity for the employment and effective utilization of technical and production personnel and facilities.
Moreover, the companies recognize their responsibility to make every effort to obtain contracts from sources in addition to the Canadian government. They are performing some work at present for the United States and other governments, and will vigorously explore ways and means of obtaining orders from the United States under the recently announced arrangements between Canada and the United States for production sharing.
If the companies are to be in a position to develop new programs and designs and to accept and fulfil contracts for production, they must retain the essential nucleus of their design, research and technical staff. To assure this desirable end the government has agreed to share equally with the companies the payroll cost of certain technical work to be undertaken by this essential nucleus of personnel for the next six months. It is expected
that by the end of that period some of the projects of the companies should be substantially advanced.
It is the hope of the government and the companies that these combined efforts will result in a steady increase in employment.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: A. V. ROE COMPANY STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH COMPANY OFFICIALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the house will have listened with interest to the statement the minister has just made. We on this side are confirmed by that statement in our view that these discussions which have been taking place in the last few days might well have been taking place months ago.

maintopic: A. V. ROE COMPANY STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH COMPANY OFFICIALS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: A. V. ROE COMPANY STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH COMPANY OFFICIALS
speechtext: If that could have been done, then the further study now being given to the proposals from the company might have resulted in action before the cancellation of the Arrow program. We notice also, Mr. Speaker, that the proposals have been made by the company. Perhaps while these studies are going on now, after the cancellation, the government itself might be able to make some proposals for the continuance of this work.

maintopic: A. V. ROE COMPANY STATEMENT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH COMPANY OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the Minister of Finance this morning will, I am afraid, mean little comfort to the 14,000 people who have been affected by lay-offs, because the only real substance of his statement was that the payroll for a certain nucleus of skilled persons would be shared equally by the government and the company. If those negotiations had taken place months ago we would not, I am certain, face this crisis which is presently faced in the aircraft industry. I urge the government to continue talks with the company and to keep on with negotiations until a solution is found and this very important industry saved for Canada. I would urge the government to exert even greater pressure on the United States to obtain for this country a fair share of production orders.
Mr. Speaker, we are encouraged that the government is talking with the company. We hope such talks will continue, but the statement of the Minister of Finance, while it is helpful in that it goes in the right direction, is certainly no answer to his very important question.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: VICTORIAVILLE, QUE.-STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR ADDITIONAL SUPPLIES OF COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska and the hon. member for Lapointe asked me about the basis of allocation of our new issues of stamps, and implied we were not meeting the demand. The house will understand, of course, that these questions reflect the popularity of the attractive new stamp designs of the present government as compared with those of our predecessors, when similar problems did not seem to arise.
With the golden anniversary of flight issue, which is the present one, we introduced a new policy of automatically allocating such new issues to every accounting post office in Canada in quantities estimated to be sufficient to permit their sale over a 10-day period. That policy was introduced on my own suggestion because I found on my field trips that many of the smaller post offices did not specifically order the new issues. I felt that the significance of their message should be carried into every part of our country.

Inquiries of the Ministry
However, if the post offices wish more than their allocation they are perfectly free to order whatever quantity is desired, either before the stamp is issued or when they are required, as long as our stock lasts. I understand that the post offices about which I have been questioned have received sufficient stocks to meet the expected demands, and additional stock is available when required.
I might add that the popularity of these new stamps has made it necessary for us to have increasing quantities printed. The 1958 quantities, which started at 15 million for the first issue were gradually raised to 25 million for the last. This year 30 million were printed for the current issue, which is the first this year, and 32 million will be printed for our NATO stamp, which will be the second issue this year.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister for some enlightenment on a matter that has caused me some concern for a number of years. When organizations such as the New Vista housing society in Burnaby and other like organizations apply for loans to provide low cost rental units, they are able to get 66968-9-92
National Housing Act
assistance under the National Housing Act. However, when they want to build a convalescent home or a home for elderly people who do not require hospital care but who yet require some nursing care, and apply for a mortgage under the terms of the National Housing Act, they are told that this type of project cannot be entertained under the provisions of the act.
I know that by now a number of organizations have asked for such assistance. I do not know whether or not they have formally applied. I happen to be on the board of directors of the British Columbia teachers' housing co-operative. At the present time we are engaged in building a project to house elderly teachers who need nursing care, and we shall be obliged to obtain our money on the open market at such a high interest rate that it will add considerably to the level of rentals. From speaking to the late E. E. Winch I know he went through the same hardship in building the first convalescent unit, if it could be called that, of the New Vista housing association.
Has any consideration been given by either the senior officials or the minister or both in consultation to extending the terms of the act in such a way that such projects might be undertaken and might obtain the benefit of the low interest money that is available? As the minister well knows, in all parts of Canada there is an urgent need for homes at rentals as low as possible where people can spend the last one, two or three years of their lives.
At the present time the only places to which these people can go are the privately owned and operated nursing homes. In the first place they are obliged to charge extremely high rates, running up to $300 and more per month. The minister knows that we have many of these privately owned homes. In the second place the waiting list for admission to these homes is extremely long. Some homes have had people waiting for a year.
Also, as the minister knows, the unfortunate and regrettable fact is that many of these homes are most inadequate. While some of them render excellent service-and I would not want to be misunderstood-there are also a fair number of them which are nothing but operations which are less than desirable, both from the standpoint of the fees they charge and the standpoint of the services they render to our elderly people. Has the minister ever given any consideration to extending the terms and conditions so these projects might be included along with regular low rental units?

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
This question has been raised on different occasions down through the years

National Housing Act
and has been carefully considered by the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, by my predecessor, Hon. Robert H. Winters and by myself. The hon. member will realize that the National Housing Act is an act designed to provide homes in which people can live. It was never meant to provide nursing homes or convalescent homes. I think these come under the scope of health and welfare departments. They are particularly a provincial responsibility.
The problem in connection with opening up the act to include convalescent homes of this type is this. Where do we stop? I think the result would be a diminution in the money that could be spent on housing, in addition to the causing of many other problems which are certainly not the concern of the officials administering the National Housing Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the act now
covers the building of senior citizens' homes, but those homes must be of the detached type. I am wondering if the act cannot be extended to cover the boarding house type of senior citizens' homes? I have one particular case in mind in West Summerland.

There the municipality is willing to guarantee bonds, and all the rest, behind it, and I am wondering if the act can be extended to cover the boarding house type of senior citizens' homes?

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

The National Housing Act
confines activities of the corporation to individual housing units. We are not able to go into the boarding house business under the terms of the act.

speechtext:
I wonder if the minister
could tell us if it would be possible to remove the provision in the present act whereby when an insured loan is sold to other than an approved lender, the insurance becomes void. subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is basic in
the insurance principle covering these loans that the loan must be administered by an approved lender or by the corporation itself. Apparently the thinking behind that was that the insurance should not be available where anybody at large was administering the loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think it is basic at
all, Mr. Chairman. I can see the disadvantage of allowing anyone at all to apply at the outset for an insured loan, because the corporation has to deal with a limited number of organizations, and organizations with which it is familiar; and just from the standpoint of red tape and mechanics it would not be possible to allow applications for insured loans from individuals or people who are not approved lenders. subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: The principle is this, that with the insurance behind the loan then the corporation will have to make good if there are losses under the loan. If the loan is being administered by someone who does not administer it properly, then that person will not suffer the loss; the loss will have to be paid out of the insurance fund.

The corporation's feeling is that only approved lenders are capable of

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: Evidently this was the thinking when the act was passed. Mind you, I admit at once that in many cases, perhaps in most cases, a person who had a mortgage would administer it properly, just as well as one of the approved lenders. But if it were opened right up and this restriction removed without any qualification, then of course anyone who bought the mortgage would have the benefit of the insurance whether he administered the mortgage properly or not.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with your permission I would like to revert to the boarding house type of senior citizens' accommodation. My reason for so doing is that I have had a little bit of experience with regard to the actual construction of the boarding house type of home. We in Oliver, a town in British Columbia where I live, did construct a boarding house type of senior citizens' home and it has been most successful.
There were many reasons for choosing it. First of all, probably the most important reason was the fact that the actual over-all cost of construction per bed was considerably lower. We tried at that time to get federal aid under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but could not do so. West Sum-merland, the other town which wants to put in a boarding house type of home, favour it simply because they feel that the cost of construction would save an awful lot of money and they could do it. There is another reason, of course, and that is that the means of control in the house, looking after people and all the rest of it, is much cheaper.
My point is that the government will provide funds under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the detached type of dwelling. Having in principle decided that they will help those people, then surely it would be common sense to provide the same accommodation at a cheaper rate. That is the whole purpose behind my question. You have a more favourable type of accommodation, so why not go into the business? I feel that C.M.H.C. is basing this decision simply on security. In other words, if the dwelling does go broke in years to come, then their security is safe because with the detached type of house they can sell it, rent it, or do what they like with it. With the boarding house type, of course, that is not so. But in the case of West Summerland, British Columbia, which proposes this type of boarding house for senior citizens, it would seem that the whole project is backed and guaranteed by West Summerland and it would only seem reasonable that the government, 66968-9-924
National Housing Act
if they are not prepared to do so at the present time, should look into this in the future as a means of providing accommodation which is necessary in Canada at the present time and is becoming increasingly more necessary.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
I am pleased to note that the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary has made an observation along the lines of some remarks which I myself had made previously. The whole purpose of this act, as the minister will agree, is to assist Canadians with their housing problems. I do not think we should be too much concerned about the particular type of housing involved.
When I say that, I have in mind a warning sounded by Mr. Mansur in reply to a question put to him by the hon. member for Eglinton during a sitting of the banking and commerce committee on February 11, 1954.

National Housing Act
At page 147 of the proceedings Mr. Mansur, in answer to the hon. member for Eglinton, had this to say:
I think, Mr. Fleming, that the very sharp increase in home ownership in Canada of which everyone seems so proud has as one of its components a fair amount of "forced home ownership" of which we should not be so proud.
This raises the problem of what kind of housing is the most valuable from a social standpoint and, I might also add, from the standpoint of our municipalities; and I often wonder whether we are very wise in making our arrangements in such a way that many people who should be renting homes are being put into the position of forced home ownership, as Mr. Mansur warned. We find people living 18 or 20 miles away from the centres of our cities, people living on the outskirts, who according to all the rules of economics should be tenants living nearer the hearts of our centres of population.
When the minister says that hitherto loans on such projects as housing for university students, accommodation for boarding elderly Canadians and accommodation for chronically sick cases could not be considered under the terms of the act, the minister should carefully consider whether these proposals are not also a manner of offering housing to Canadians. It should not really matter to us whether this housing is in the form of boarding houses or residences for students or places where the chronically ill elderly people may live, or whether it is in the form of individually owned homes of the kind which today cause so many headaches because of the manner in which new housing subdivisions are being developed.
I think the minister might well consider a change in basic policy here. I realize full well the validity of the minister's argument when he points out that housing for chronically ill people is basically the responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare and especially of the health and welfare departments of the provinces. I also know that our national hospital plan provides for federal assistance to provincial governments if they will undertake to build hospitals to look after chronically ill patients. However, I believe the minister also knows- and if he has not yet been informed I hope he will note this fact-that the government of British Columbia while on the one hand encouraging all municipalities to begin building hospitals for the chronically ill has thus far flatly refused to give any financial assistance toward the building of such hospitals, even though financial assistance is available through the federal government. The provincial government is apparently unwilling to

pass on the assistance available from the federal authority, and unwiling to make its own contribution.
The need is real, and it is most urgent. 1 hope the minister can see his way clear to reconsider his position and take the attitude that the whole purpose of the National Housing Act is to provide accommodation for the people of Canada, and that it will not necessarily be designed for assistance toward individual home ownership. I think the problem is more complex than that.
I should like to raise a second point at this time with respect to housing for senior citizens under the National Housing Act. Under the provisions of this legislation this government makes loans only toward the building of such units. However, as the minister knows, some of the provincial governments instead of making loans offer outright assistance. In British Columbia, the minister's home province, the provincial government pays one-third of the capital cost. I believe the day is long overdue when the senior government should consider using the act in such manner that it can make an outright donation to equal at least the donation made by any provincial government, instead of offering loans for capital construction which must be repaid with interest, thereby increasing rental costs.
I should also like to ask the minister if he is able to issue a renewed assurance that interest rates under this act will not be raised in the year ahead. As the minister is well aware, the interest rates on long term federal government borrowings have always been a determining factor in interest rates charged under this act. These rates have been rising for a considerable length of time, and I believe present federal rates are only one-hundredth of one per cent short of an all-time high since the Bank of Canada was first established. There is abroad the apprehension that if federal interest rates on long term borrowings remain this high or go higher the operating margin left to the officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will become so narrow that the interest rate payable under the terms of the National Housing Act will be increased.
I believe the Canadian people would like the minister to make a statement on the matter at this time. I know how happy we were about six months ago when he assured us that for the time being at least there would be no increase in the interest rates allowable under this act.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is one that I raised last year. I was very interested in hearing the hon. member for Nip-issing ask for information concerning what

is happening under the insurance fund. I do not think the minister could be accused of having been persuaded of the correctness of the socialist approach, but I feel he would be exercising sound common sense in looking after the welfare of people who acquire homes under the act if he would give serious consideration to amending the insurance feature in such a way that monthly payments on homes purchased under the act would be paid in periods when the home owner is unemployed.
This may seem a fantastic idea to some Conservatives, but may I point out that many automobile agents are now advertising automobiles on the monthly payment plan and included in the terms of sale is a condition that any monthly payment falling due while the prospective car owner is unemployed will be automatically paid out of the insurance fund. We have many thousands of unemployed Canadians who are experiencing difficulty in meeting the monthly payments on their homes, and a cause of serious concern to them must be how long they will be able to continue without making regular monthly payments. Payments on homes during periods of unemployment could be included in the insurance feature. I also believe the government should consider providing life insurance for the purchasers of homes, and also insurance for payments during periods of complete and total disability.
If private companies can initiate schemes of this kind in their efforts to promote sales I do not think it is too much to expect the federal government to begin offering somewhat similar terms and conditions to purchasers of homes under the National Housing Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would hesitate to take the lead in bringing about a system whereby the National Housing Act was administered in the same way as the sales of automobiles. If we ever adopted that system of financing I am sure of one thing, and that is that homes would cost the Canadian people a great deal more than they cost today.
The hon. member mentioned that everything was being done for home owners but very little for people who live in apartments but this, of course, is not the case at all. There are millions and millions of dollars being put out under the National Housing Act for rental accommodation. This money is being expended in different ways. For instance, it is available under the insurance provisions. Loans are not limited to homes that are individually owned, and in many cases loans are made for apartment buildings. There were 7,000 units started last year under the limited dividend provisions of the
National Housing Act
act. In the dominion-provincial loans scheme these, too, are all for rental accommodation; and for several months under the agency plan we were making direct loans to builders for apartment accommodation. Mind you, as the funds became low we restricted these loans to homes, but millions and millions of dollars have been provided under the provisions of the act for rental accommodation.
The hon. member said that Mr. Mansur had made a statement to the effect that there was some reason to doubt the wisdom of what he described as "forced home ownership". I have not read the statement made by Mr. Mansur, but I would doubt that it contained all the implications the hon. member mentioned. His suggestion appeared to imply that people should be forced to live in the centre of cities. The hon. member suggested we were getting too many homes in the suburbs, and that we should make people live downtown in rented accommodation. One of the reasons Canada has grown into a great, strong, young nation has been that to such a large degree it is a nation of home owners. Everyone in this chamber today who has had to start out and acquire a home of his own and dig the garden-I know in my own case I had to wheel rocks from all over vacant lots to make a rockery, and I might say that the rocks in Vancouver are mighty big-is of necessity a good citizen with a sense of pride in home ownership and a strong feeling of identification with his local community. When you own a home your roots go down. You take pride in that home, and it contributes to your feeling of happiness and well-being. I believe it is just human nature to respond in this fashion.
The hon. member expressed the opinion that it is a bad thing to have so many homes in the suburbs, and he referred to those individually owned homes causing headaches of all kinds. Well, they may cause worries to municipal authorities and transportation authorities and possibly in other ways, but we are a nation of free people. Canadians are at liberty to make their own choice, and they do not have to buy a house if they do not want to. Certainly in the last year they have shown every indication that they want to buy houses, and they want to buy small houses.
I have the figures here for the starts in the month of January. On an earlier occasion I gave the starts for the calendar year 1958. Starts to the number of 4,790 were made during the month as compared with January, 1958 when the figure was 3,945. This is an increase of 21.4 per cent. These are not completions, they are starts. If we had the figure for completions, naturally it would be

National Housing Act
much higher because there were many more houses started last year. These are brand new starts for the month of January.
Then, in so far as people not wanting to buy houses or not wanting to own houses is concerned, there again the figures for January are very reassuring. The number of completed and unoccupied houses at the end of January, 1959 showed a decline from the previous year in spite of the fact that thousands and thousands more houses were built last year than in any other period in Canada's history. The figures are 3,010 as of January 31, 1959; 3,190 as of January 31, 1958. The figure is very reassuring. Housing in Canada is very, very successful at the present time. I think Canadians from coast to coast realize that fact.
Naturally we are very interested in any suggestions for the improvement of the housing policy. We try not to close our minds to suggestions of any kind, but my good friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam can rest assured that in Canada the housing picture is not too bad at the present time, and that the officials of the corporation and the government will endeavour to keep closely in touch with developments and change the policy as needs may require.
He mentioned the interest rate. There is no intention of raising the interest rate. That should be made clear at the present time. He is quite right in bringing that up. I think if he were responsible for housing policy he himself would hesitate to branch out into all those other proposals such as providing life insurance and nursing accommodation. After all, it was nursing accommodation and not housing that he mentioned. This also applies to going into the various other fields. We try to get into just as much as we can possibly handle in a sensible way. I think the housing program in Canada today and also under the former government-I am not claiming all the credit for the present government-is a policy which is typically Canadian and which has been succeeding very well.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a little difficulty being seen down here. I wanted to bring one or two suggestions to the attention of the minister before the bill passes. I was particularly gratified to hear the minister's remarks on the putting down of roots and the resulting good citizenship which accrues thereby. It seems to us in the Yukon, at least in the past, that a good many policies such as the housing policy of the federal government have sort of by-passed the people up there. It simply does not work.
A good example of that, as I am sure the minister is aware, is the fact that since the

housing act has been in existence only three or four units have been constructed by private individuals. The reason for this is quite apparent, namely that transportation costs to those northern areas simply increase the cost of construction to the point where it is simply beyond the means of the average income earner. A house which would cost $10,000 or $11,000 to build in Edmonton or Winnipeg would cost as much as $14,000 or $15,000 in the north.
As the minister knows, a family man with three children cannot get along in a house in the cost bracket of $9,000 or $10,000. He needs a three bedroom house, and in the northern areas this usually runs him up into the neighbourhood of $14,000. This house in the Yukon, at any rate, would end up costing him between $18,000 and $20,000. Even when you apply the maximum loan of $12,800 it can readily be seen how far beyond the capabilities of the average income earner this house is. He simply is not able to raise the down payment.
The minister has said that in Canada housing is very successful. From my own observations, and from listening to his remarks and the remarks of most other hon. members, 1 can fully realize this. I think it is very successful in the rest of Canada; but with all due deference to the minister-and I believe through no direct fault of his own-this success has not yet extended to the northern areas of Canada.
I said I was particularly interested in hearing the minister's remarks concerning the putting down of roots because, like him, I believe it does make for good citizenship. I might go further and say that unless the family man can look to good housing as well as to health and education facilities in many of those pioneer communities, and the possibility of obtaining them, we in the north will not get that type of permanent settlement that is desirable. One of the best methods of providing that facility to the individual who wishes to go north is by providing it under the provisions of the National Housing Act.
I understand that in some of the provinces there are schemes available which will allow an individual who wishes to build a house to draw on provincial funds for the purpose of bridging the gap between his down payment and the down payment required by the National Housing Act. I may be wrong here, but I believe some such scheme exists in Ontario.
I have this suggestion to make to the minister. I am sure he is well aware of the fact that the Yukon territorial government cannot afford to put up funds for this purpose. It might be possible, however, for the minister,

in co-operation with his colleague the minister of northern affairs, to arrange that funds be made available to the territorial government through the federal government for this purpose. A fund of this nature would enable the individual in the north to be assisted in raising the down payment necessary to bring himself within the terms of the National Housing Act.
Many hon. members might wonder why this suggestion concerning a fund should be made at all. I put this suggestion forward rather than suggest that the act be amended to accommodate special circumstances which are applicable in the north. An act which is national in scope cannot be amended to cover regional difficulties. I quite understand this. However, somehow or other this gap must be bridged. This suggestion of setting up a fund to assist the individual in the north will, I think, achieve that objective.
Now, the difficulties with regard to building in the north are many, and if we are to achieve any degree of permanency about the settlements, if we are to attract people to the north to achieve that degree of settlement which is essential to the proper development of the north, then we must look in the direction of providing those people who wish to go to the north with the amenities, perhaps not all the amenities but at least the bare essentials that are available to their fellow citizens in the south.
I shall terminate these remarks with the observation that in the opinion of the people in the Yukon, the housing act which has been so successful in providing homes for families with average incomes in the south, and in providing low rental and low cost accommodation, has certainly not been available to them. They have been working under a handicap. The turnover in population has been large. The inducements to settlement have been poor, and one of the areas in which improvement could definitely be made is in the area of housing.
Already, through his department and in co-operation with his colleague the minister of northern affairs as well as officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the minister has made available to municipalities in the Yukon a scheme whereby low rental units may be constructed. I understand that the municipality of Whitehorse has already initiated plans to take advantage of this scheme. I am now speaking of low cost housing and plans which would enable the individual to acquire his own home which, because of the many factors I have described, is impossible at the moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
These are very interesting comments that the hon. member for Yukon has
National Housing Act
made. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation adds 20 per cent to the Yukon appraisal rates but the loans, of course, are subject to the statutory maximum of $12,800. It might be wise if the Yukon council were to make some recommendation with regard to this policy. As the hon. member knows, there is now limited self-government for the Yukon and I have not heard that the council has made any suggestion that provision should be made for second mortgages on homes in the Yukon. This policy is in effect in the province of Quebec, but not in Ontario. It may also be in effect in some of the other provinces. It seems to me that would be a better way of making provision to meet this need than to try to amend the National Housing Act so that one provision was available for the Yukon and a different provision for the rest of Canada.

speechtext: Of course I did not suggest that the act be amended, and I said that was why I made the alternative suggestion. I referred to the difficulty in amending an act national in scope to apply to any particular region. I think the figures we have just been given are ample proof that the corporation should give consideration to lowering the rate on insurance. I know the overall amount of money involved is large, but it seems to me that if, as I understand, there has been a debit of only $99,000 since 1954, while in the last year alone this insurance fund has been supplemented by something of the order of $15 million, then the insurance fee could be lowered.
Mention of this fact leads me to the main problem, I think, in connection with housing today. I do not want to take away from what has been accomplished in this last record year, but I think everyone will agree that one of the main problems in the industry today is the increased cost of housing. I do

National Housing Act not think there is anything quite so alarming to those who are concerned with the low income group, and there is no one in any corner of the house who has any priority in interest in this group. It seems to me our housing legislation is not fulfilling the need for which it was originally designed, that is the need for housing in what is sometimes referred to as the lower half of the income scale.
As I say, I am not seeking to detract from anything the government is doing at the present time, but this is a very real problem. I wondered what thoughts the minister may care to express today as to what the government may be doing to try to bring down the cost of housing. We know that each year there seems to be a continuing spiral of rising costs. We are not suggesting controls or anything of that sort, because we are well aware of the problem. I wondered if the government had given any thought to setting up a committee or a study group perhaps within the framework of the corporation, or one that would include officials of the corporation and some of the best brains of industry, finance and representatives of provincial and municipal governments. Perhaps some serious study could be given to this problem of rising costs.
I recall that not long ago an outstanding spokesman for the house building industry in Toronto made the statement that before long all houses in that particular area were going to cost $20,000 or more. This is a real problem, and it is preventing people in the lower income group from getting houses. I could not agree more with the minister- notwithstanding all that is being done in connection with limited dividend schemes and so on; they are all very good and should be encouraged-that there is no substitute for the man owning his own home. I think most people recognize the fact that it is becoming increasingly difficult for him to do so with these rising costs.
There is another problem to which I referred briefly here on Wednesday. Some means must be found to narrow the gap between the cost of these homes and the amount of the loans. I think these two problems are the major ones we are facing today. I wonder whether the minister would care to comment on them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

speechtext:
I think there is a good deal of wishful thinking when it is suggested that any government should bring down the price of homes. It is easy to make that suggestion; and of course the federal government is always the last government to which people run in order to have it do all these things.
The hon. member suggests that the federal government should bring down the price of homes. After all, we live in a free country. As I said the other day, we have no intention of putting a ceiling on wages or of controlling prices. They have all been going up. The wage earners have been getting higher wages-and I am not quarrelling with that fact-and people have been getting higher prices for their goods. The corporation has been doing everything possible to keep down the price of homes. This is one of the main worries the officials have. In addition to that, each year the Canadian Construction Association, which also is greatly interested in this problem, has a conference in Ottawa to which are called representatives of many different fields of interest in housing, and extremely useful work has been done in this regard.
The hon. member will realize that the small home loan policy puts a limit on the size of a home. There are also many other restrictions. Many of the frills cannot be put into these homes if a loan is to be obtained. People like to have frills. They like to have the modern conveniences. I expect they are going to continue to like to have them. The price of homes simply cannot just be set at a certain figure and stopped from rising. The situation, of course, is far worse in a city like metropolitan Toronto. The problem is not nearly as great in the smaller centres of Canada. We are doing everything we can to try to keep the prices down.
In thinking of the debates that have taken place this session on the subject of housing, I am afraid the impression has gone out that nobody with a small income can get any help whatever under the National Housing Act. This is far from the truth. Over 13 per cent of the people benefiting under the small home loan policy have been in the income group from $3,000 to $4,000 a year. If more homes were built in the rural areas or in the small towns there would be a much larger percentage, but the people in those areas are not seeking new homes to the same extent as are people in the metropolitan areas. One reason that the figures look high is that so many houses have been going into the metropolitan areas like metropolitan Toronto. It is figured now that the lower half income group are from $4,500 a year down; that is for

family income. We are therefore getting well down into the lower income groups with our housing policy.
Another thing is that in respect of many of the loans for small amounts, we find that the borrowers do not want to put into a home the percentage of their income that they are allowed to put into it under the regulations. They can put in up to 27 per cent on the cost of a home; that is for the carrying charges on a home. However, there is fairly clear indication that in the lower income groups the buyers do not want to put that much in. Of course they are free to make their own arrangements. They are not forced to put in 27 per cent. If they did so, of course, it would mean that buyers with smaller incomes would be able to benefit under the provisions of the act. However, these are all extremely helpful suggestions that hon. members are making, and we will certainly give them careful consideration.

I am very much in order,
because I am referring to the minister in his capacity as the member of the government responsible for the administration of this act. The minister has told us that housing is going on very successfully at the present time, and I agree with him that this act is aiding those whose incomes are above average and, more lately, even those of average income, to satisfy their needs for housing in the dominion of Canada. We have no quarrel with that, and the minister is very wrong when he says that I attempted to imply that it was a bad thing to have many people living in the suburbs. I hope I did not say that; I hope I did not imply it. I hope I did not imply that I favoured any policy which would make people live downtown, to use the minister's words.
I have read through Hansard and I find that all the thinking represented in the ideas or suggestions offered the minister within 66968-9-93J
National Housing Act
recent days follow the same line; that is, how can we assist to increase the possibility of home ownership. All the arguments tend to be in that direction and even some of the changes in regulations under the act are inclined that way. I warned the minister a year ago about the danger of reducing the standards or minimum requirements as to the size of future houses in Canada. At that time I believe I said that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation might find itself responsible for the building of areas that will be future slums. I regret the tendency to reduce standards and minimum requirements in order to encourage more Canadians to become home owners.
The minister has received many proposals one of which was that the period of amortization be increased. All the thinking in this house seems channelled in the direction of what can be done to enable more Canadians to buy homes of their own with the hope of eventually owning them. I appreciate that the minister has some conception of economics. As I indicated before, he has one of the sharpest minds in the government. I know he has heard of a fundamental law of economics, the point of maximum return. I am not so sure that that point has not already been reached if not exceeded in this policy of encouraging an increasing number of Canadians to become owners of their own homes.
I know the government is opposed to subsidized ownership of homes and I am afraid that like its predecessor it is also opposed to subsidized rental as a basic principle. We in this group see nothing wrong with subsidization in either field if it is in the national interest. I believe the minister knows full well that private enterprise has found it no longer profitable to build homes for rental purposes with the exception of luxury apartment suites. There was a day when it used to pay an individual to invest his life's savings in the building of an additional home for the purpose of renting it. He could safely count on receiving $1 per month in rental for every $100 of his investment. That situation no longer applies in Canada and in fact it has not applied for some years. Rarely today does a Canadian invest his life's savings in the building of homes for rental purposes. That is done now usually only in the case of superdeluxe apartment blocks where extraordinarily high rentals can be charged.
When we consider that private enterprise has completely deserted the home rental field so far as ordinary Canadians are concerned it can be seen that we have a problem on our hands. That is what Mr. Mansur the former president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was referring to as I indicated

National Housing Act
this morning when he said that there is a danger in forced home ownership. Mr. Mansur pointed out that this problem does not exist in French Canada but in English Canada. At page 148 of the report to which I have referred he is reported as having said:
One other major difference in English-speaking Canada which I think has an influence is that there is not the landlord class in English-speaking Canada that there is in French-speaking Canada. The entrepreneurs in that field are not intrested as they are in the province of Quebec. Further, in English-speaking Canada we do not have that big sector of the most efficient rental housing of all-
I should like to underline this opinion of Mr. Mansur.
-the most efficient rental housing of all, the duplex and the triplex where the owner lives in the bottom unit and is a resident landlord in respect to the one or two units above him. This is the ultimate in efficiency in managing rental property. This does not exist in the other parts of the country.
Mr. Mansur went on to say:
I think that every effort should be devoted, as we are trying to, to encourage entrepreneurs is the residential field to get into activities like row housing-a form of rental housing which would be satisfactory to the English-speaking Canadian housewife and yet be economical for management by the landlord.
I believe those words are worthy of serious consideration by the minister in determining the administration of this act. In addition to the major point I have attempted to make that the act has not been too successful in meeting what may well be the major housing need of the Canadian public at this time and that is accommodation on a rental basis at modest rates.
I should like to ask the minister how far the present amendments to the act are intended to go or may go toward eliminating the existing racket in the mortgage field. 1 am sure the minister knows very well what it is to which I have reference. Are these amendments designed in any way to eliminate the regrettable occurrence on the Canadian scene where first mortgages are offered for sale at discounts as high as 25 per cent and second mortgages are offered as high as 50 per cent? I am sure the minister would agree that most of this negotiable paper being offered for sale is new paper. They are planned and plotted in advance of the building of the houses. We have a very unfortunate case in New Westminster, as the minister well knows, which is now before the courts and I may not debate it here. But I am pleased to see that at long last one of those cases has been hauled up before the courts for a judicial decision.
I also noted the minister's announcement that he is not contemplating any rise in interest rates in the future. I am very

happy and I think millions of Canadians will be very happy with that announcement. Can we assume as a result of the minister's announcement that, in the interests of more housing for Canadians, this government will be prepared to meet an operating loss on the part of management of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation? I think this is a vital answer to both management of the corporation and to our concern as to how long a period of time we may expect the minister's announcement on interest rates to remain valid.
I suppose the minister forgot to indicate his reaction to my plea that this government at least match what the provincial governments are doing and that they make a grant toward the provision of housing for senior citizens at least equal to the grant of one-third of the capital cost now being supplied by some of the provincial governments of Canada.
The minister has gone to great lengths to emphasize that this government considers itself only in the role of a residual lender. I think the sooner it acclimatizes itself to harsh, cold economic realities the better because, as the minister very well knows, the government is no longer a residual lender; it is the major lender and the major partner; therefore, I think we should not hear very much more of that residual lender business.
We have assumed this as a responsibility of the government of Canada and I think rightly so. I think that is where it ought to belong and the sooner we adjust our thinking along those lines the better off housing will be in Canada.
At the cost of repeating, I should like to say that our basic contention is that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been tremendously successful and especially under the auspices of the minister who is responsible at the present time. However, our contention is that most of the help has gone to those who really do not need the help of the taxpayers of Canada, and that those who need the help of the community at large for the purpose of ownership, and especially in the rental field, have been left without the assistance that was originally announced as being the aims and objects of this act when it was first introduced in the House of Commons.

There are several points I want to raise in connection with this legislation. I imagine that the minister is familiar with one of them through the hon. member for Scarborough. It relates to the problem in connection with the area known as Stapleford farm. I am going to relate this matter to the bill very shortly. As the minister is aware, there has been going on in the Scarborough region a controversy that has two aspects.
One is the fact that people in privately developed subdivisions are up in arms over this Stapleford farm development because they have paid approximately $2,100 or $2,200 for their property, and it appears that people in an adjoining area putting up their own homes under the land settlement scheme can get their lots for $800 or $900. This has caused hard feelings.
The other aspect is that there is this feeling, which is supported by a letter I have here written to the Hon. William Nickle by the education director for Scarborough, that figures which have been released in connection with this plan have not been fair in that they do not show that where you have rental units you have the type of families where there are more children than usual, and so you have an extra burden on the school cost. I thought the hon. member for Scarborough could take a certain pride in the position which he took at certain public meetings in the area when this controversy developed, but I would like to know what the hon. minister and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials intend to do in this particular field to try and straighten out this problem, which promises to be a developing one.
An animosity is developing between people in private subdivisions and these land settlement plans with rental units, and I would like to ask if there will be any consideration given to tackling this educational side of the problem. In a city like Port Arthur or Fort William it would not be a particular problem, because you have one educational authority; but where you have a cluster of educational authorities, a rental housing scheme means that there may be a funnelling and concentration into that area of an inordinate number of children, and so the school costs go up inordinately. This is a real problem, and I

would like to suggest that the figures in connection with what the federal government is spending in the metropolitan areas are really disappointing.
The Lawrence park development, the Regent park south development and the Scarborough development really add up to a pittance in terms of rental housing in comparison with the great wen which has been growing at Toronto. All the good intentions in the world which have been expressed by the hon. minister and the previous minister are not going to give a real, dynamic lead in this particular rental field. The hon. member for Welland has already made the point that this matter is an important one. I do not think the minister has given us enough indication that his department, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and this legislation is going to have any particular effect in this field. I would ask that he consider very seriously what can be done to head off these developing conflicts between people who may have National Housing Act loans themselves but who look over at a subdivision where you have rental units, which in turn gets their backs up. As I believe the hon. member for Scarborough pointed out at public meetings, this injects a sort of class distinction into the community which is bad; but more than that, it is beginning to put an opprobrium on rental housing just at the very time when that is a topic the federal and provincial governments should be attacking.
The other point I wanted to bring up arises from an answer which I received on January 19 from the corporation, through the minister, relating to foreclosures. I was very pleased with the information supplied in this answer, and I wondered why the hon. minister or the corporation did not make more of it. We have had only a total, I think, of eleven mortgages which had to be foreclosed in 1958 under the National Housing Act. I want to point out in this connection that on June 12 of last year Mr. Bates, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, was reported to have told a Senate committee, in relation to mortgages being in arrears:
The situation is not dangerous yet, but in many parts of the country there is evidence of people being in difficulties.
I would suggest that the information which has been tabled indicates that the fears of Mr. Bates have not quite been realized. This article, reported in a press release from the Ottawa bureau of the Globe and Mail dated June 12, points out that there is a reserve fund of approximately $30 million, built up as insurance against these loans collapsing. Mr. Bates went on to say:

All seven claims made on the fund arose from foreclosures necessitated by a disruption of the borrower's family-
In other words, these were very special circumstances.
The corporation sold the houses involved and actually made a profit of more than $4,000 on the seven transactions. This profit went into the insurance fund but if any of the original borrowers turned up, he would have a claim on any profit made on the sale of his house.
The point I want to make is that according to the evidence filed the foreclosures have been so few that the reserve fund must be in a strong position. I would like to know why the minister last year took exception to members asking questions about a moratorium on foreclosures of mortgages. Does not the very stability of the whole operation and the fact there is still little pressure on the reserve fund indicate that there should be lower interest rates? It seems to me that should be one of the chief arguments in support of that proposition. If there are so few foreclosures, and the people getting involved in this type of housing are so trustworthy, why cannot we see some advantage accruing out of that situation? I know that the hon. minister cannot foresee a continuation of this recession; I am sure he is one of the persons who would tell us we are moving on to bigger and better times and that things are going ahead. Mr. Chairman, I believe I can speak with a little authority on the subject of housing for senior citizens for, as the minister knows, my late father as a member of the provincial legislature of British Columbia started the first project of this kind in that province. I may say he always received the greatest assistance and co-operation from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As a matter of fact, on that project we now have approximately three-quarters of a million dollars worth of housing and although it breaks my heart a little to say it we still owe Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation approximately $387,000.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam raised a question which I think deserves sympathic understanding and perhaps comment on the part of the minister. As was pointed out by the minister it is possible to borrow money from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at less than the usual rate for projects of this kind. Approximately seven or eight years ago when the projects were started in British Columbia it was possible to supply senior citizens with an excellent modern home or apartment at a rental for a couple of approximately $21.50 or $22.50 a month, if my memory is correct. Because of increased costs of construction and repairs it is no longer possible to provide accommodation at that rate.
What is not generally recognized by the majority of people and often not by the tenants themselves is that the basis of the rental is not established by organizations in this field such as New Vista, Canadian Legion or the United Church but rather it is established by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The corporation checks each year on the administration and financing and sets the rental. The corporation has almost complete control but I do not question this because it does advance money at lower rates of interest than could otherwise be obtained. Whereas a few years ago it was possible to make homes or apartments available at the rental I mentioned it is now necessary to charge up to $35 a month for new accommodation. The modest increase in old age pensions and the lower dollar value results in the senior citizens being penalized. In view of the fact that the government of

National Housing Act
British Columbia has contributed not less than one-third of the capital cost as an outright grant and in view of increasing costs confronting our senior citizens is it not possible for the federal government to bring rentals more in line with the ability of senior citizens to pay?

speechtext: If the minister will check with his officials I believe he will find that any change in rental as a result of the increased cost of administration, decoration or repairs has to be authorized by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. No change may be made without the authority of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: If the operating costs, not of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but of the limited dividend corporations go up they have to take the responsibility of applying and getting the approval of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation before they can increase the rent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
I have no objection to that.
I have been connected with these projects in British Columbia since their inception. We are proud of the housing we have and as I said it amounts to approximately three-quarters of a million dollars worth of construction.
I am simply pointing out to the minister that because of increasing construction costs and the increasing costs of administration, decorating and repairs the associations carrying on that kind of work with the consent and authority of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to remain in the black as they must be are having to raise the rents. I know that we could rent these houses or apartments for $125 or $150 a month if they were on the market. The rental of this accommodation is now as high as $35 a month and because of increasing costs and a lessened dollar value it is out of the range of many senior citizens. We are simply asking if it is not possible for the federal government to make a contribution at least equal to that made by the provinces thereby enabling the associations involved in this field to bring down the rentals.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: This would mean a new policy right across the country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: Of course.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

has been no such request from the Canadian Legion. They have some low rental housing projects in Vancouver as have many of the service clubs. subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: That is all I ask.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was rather
amazed at the approach taken by the minister a few moments ago. First of all he deplored my mentioning the racket in the mortgage field. I was hoping he would associate himself with my attitude in this regard. The minister knows very well indeed that in his own home town first mortgages may be purchased at a 25 per cent reduction of the principal and second mortgages may be purchased for discounts running all the way up to 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: Not National Housing Act mortgages.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
I will agree with the minister at once; these are not National Housing Act mortgages, but I think the minister did not understand what I was asking. I was asking, will these proposed amendments in any way help to eliminate this racketeering that exists in the mortgage field in Canada? When I made the statement that first class mortgage rates in Canada were at least seven per cent the minister cried blue ruin and attempted to say that I was only attempting to get newspaper headlines. May I say to the minister that I know intimately one association whose assets are $1,500,000-plus, and that those people have been able to find safe investments, have been able to lend out on first mortgages even more money than they have at eight per cent, and have been able to place all the money at their disposal on first mortgages at eight per cent for many long years now.
If the minister attempts to cast any aspersions on my claim that a realistic; first mortgage rate across Canada at the present time is seven per cent I think he is very misinformed indeed because first mortgage rates by private lenders-I am not now referring to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages-are at least seven per cent. The minister is attempting to have things both ways. Since he is a British Columbian I can well understand that. We have long learned to have our cake and eat it, too. We pay off the debt of the province while our debt climbs higher than ever at the

same time. We are used to that kind of policy. However, the minister said he is absolutely opposed to a subsidy for the operations of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He made it very definite, yet at the same time the minister must know that earnings at the moment on the 1983 federal conversion bonds are approaching five per cent.
The act allows for a margin of operations to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation of 2\ per cent, which would bring the interest rate that might be charged to somewhere near seven per cent. The minister assures us that interest rates will not be raised and we love that assurance. At the same time he denies to the officials of the corporation any idea that they can count on an operating loss and retain the support of the government. I do not know what is the operating cost margin percentagewise of the corporation. I would be very happy if the minister supplied us with that information. What is the actual cost percentagewise? Is it one per cent, is it three per cent or is it two per cent? We would like to know. However, when the minister goes overboard, as he did a year ago, in attempting to create the impression that we shall have to do whatever is necessary to interest private capital into the housing field, he knows as well as I do that this means only one thing. There is only one kind of bait that will attract them unless the government is prepared to take action, namely the bait of higher returns. When the minister assures us that the return will not exceed six per cent and we know that the base is rising and we know that there must be some expenses connected with the operations of the corporation, we do not know what we are to take from that.
The minister says he will not countenance subsidizing the corporation. At the same time he says, despite all statistics to the contrary, that he will remain firm. We welcome this decision more than the other, I must say. We welcome the decision that interest rates will not be raised. We would regret very much to have to pass this legislation and one month hence read that because of market conditions it is regretted that the government has had to raise interest rates beyond the six per cent level. That is the only thing we want to be assured of. We want to be assured that if necessary the government would rather subsidize the corporation than see a further rise in the interest rates, and the minister has not yet satisfied us on this point.

Clause agreed to.

speechtext:
I want to speak for just a moment on subclause 2 of clause 3. This clause is applicable only to loans made after the coming into force of the act. The minister will recall that at the resolution stage we had a few words to say on this matter. We dealt with it at some length on second reading, therefore it is not my intention to restate the arguments I put forward at that time. I am not in any way getting away from the fact that we gave full support to this on second reading, but it does seem to me that by this subclause 2 we are creating two classes of mortgages, namely those that are guaranteed up to 98 per cent and those that are 100 per cent guaranteed.
I know that by this very legislation the government is anxious to make mortgages more negotiable. This is most desirable. It seems to me that in creating these two classes of mortgages no assistance at all is being given to the mortgages that exist today. I cannot see any real reason why a mortgage made next year should by the implementation of this act be made more desirable. A mortgage made next year will be more desirable, more negotiable than one made, say, last year. There does not seem to be really any justification for setting up two classes. Can the minister say a word on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Apparently there is some slight price differential between a mortgage on which the insurance is up to 100 per cent and one on which it is 98 per cent, but not as big a price differential as there would be between a mortgage which carried an interest rate of five per cent and one which carried a rate of six per cent.
As the hon. member knows, there are many mortgages which come under the National Housing Act which are at a rate other than six per cent and we did not feel that there was any reason why we should make a donation of two per cent on the mortgages which have already been issued.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: It does seem to me that the desire of the legislation is to make those mortgages more negotiable. I cannot come to any other conclusion than that we are setting up two distinct classes of mortgages, one more desirable than the other. It would seem to be as desirable to make mortgages that were made a year ago or two years ago as negotiable as many that may be placed in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
Of course, we have different types of mortgages because the interest rates have been different. In addition to that, one of the main purposes of this amendment is to

National Housing Act
encourage fresh money to come into the mortgage market, and it will have that effect. Anybody putting up money now will have an insurance policy which covers up to a total loss. The officials believe it would be unwise to make this retroactive to apply to all the mortgages which have already been issued by the corporation in the years gone by.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: I have just one question with respect to this particular clause. In effect, from what I can gather, it does remove any possible element of risk on the part of the investor, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: No, it may not quite do that. Hitherto, they could only be protected up to 98 per cent and now, under the amendment, they can qualify up to 100 per cent under the terms of the mortgage.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: I think probably that is what I was getting at in the first place. If a bank, for instance, or an approved lender under the act lends money, from now on after this bill is passed and receives royal assent that loan is insured and guaranteed. There is no element of risk whatever, is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: It certainly removes most of the risk. In my view, one of the main attractions of the amendment from the point of view of the corporation is that it will make it possible for trust funds to be invested in these mortgages to a far greater extent than is possible now. When the insurance coverage was only 98 per cent some of the lenders were advised that they could not put in various types of trust funds.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: The minister said it would remove most of the risks. What would be the balance left after most of the risk has been taken into account? What risk is there left?

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext: I can only give the hon. member one good example. A lawyer might charge $500 for the foreclosure and the figure that can be recovered is only $150 even when these amendments come into effect.

The minister should have
answered my question by saying "yes" in the first place. Then, we would not have had to go all around like this.

subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.

speechtext: I wonder if the minister might question his officials to see if the figures are available in a different form. I do not want to have them set up a new set of figures. It seems to me that this information must be available, in perhaps different form, but which would convey the same information I am seeking. I want to know what percentage of this $375 million went into the large centres of Canada, that is all. Perhaps I can help by asking, do they have figures for other than the centres of 50,000 I mentioned? Would they have figures for centres of 100,000 and over?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, ETC.
speechtext:
My officials say they can get this by Monday. Each week I get a return showing me the activities of the week, and the hon. member might get a sufficient indication of the split from that to satisfy him. For example, in the week ending February 20, approvals in centres of under 55,000 were $375,086; centres over 55,000, $235,619. Then, the figures for 1958-59 up to this date were, under 55,000, $37,832,531; over 55,000, $17,815,776.
In addition a great deal of the money went out to builders. There was not so much in the week ending February 20 because we cut off the loans to builders on December 31 for the reason that if the money were lent after that they would not be building in the winter, so builders' loans that had not been dealt with amounted to $51,211, and in 1958-59, builders' loans totalled $168,866,381. The figures for these loans to builders are not broken down into centres of over 55,000 or under 55,000, and this is where the officials are meeting with their difficulty. However, I think it can be taken for granted that the great bulk of the money which went into builders' loans went into the centres of over 55,000.
