Supply-Citizenship and Immigration came to the attention of and have been tabulated by the department. While precise figures are not available, it is a well-known fact that many immigrants do not seek the assistance of the department but become established very successfully on their own initiative.
Now a word about non-immigrants. Last August, in order to establish effective control over the temporary admission of persons who might seek employment in competition with Canadian residents or who sought temporary entry with a view to subsequently applying for permanent residence while actually in Canada, I announced a policy regarding the stricter application of regulations governing non-immigrant entry. In order to be fair about this, the new policy was not made retroactive and I further stated that those non-immigrants then in Canada who wished to remain here could make application for permanent admission before March 1, 1959, and if their case had merit it would be given sympathetic consideration. As expected, the department has received many applications for landing from persons who were in Canada at the time I made my announcement. Up to January 31, 1959, 3,805 applications, for permanent admission had been received from such persons. Of the 3,805 applications, a total of 2,012 have been finally dealt with and of these, 1,808, or roughly 90 per cent, have been given favourable consideration and the persons landed, while the applications of 204 have been withdrawn or refused. One thousand seven hundred and ninety-three cases were still in process as of January 31, 1959, and of these, 1,703 have been given approval in principle and landing action will follow provided the applicants can meet the normal medical standards, etc., while the merits of the remaining 90 were yet to be assessed.
I think it can be said that the new procedures seem to be accomplishing their purpose very well indeed.
Would the hon. lady permit a question?
Surely.
Were those 2,000 cases, or as many of them as have been dealt with up to December 31, included in the total of immigrants for the year, or is that 2,000 more?
The figure I gave you was up to January 31; but those who were landed prior to December 31 were included in the figures of immigrants for last year.
In other words, there were 122,800 new immigrants instead of 124,800: that is the point.

I have not got the figures here up to December 31. They are round figures. The 2,012 figure is up to January 31, and I think there were 1,700 up to the end of December. But that is the general idea.
At present, as was the case in 1958, stress is laid on encouraging the admission of suitable and desirable persons with capital or other means of self-establishment who have a sincere desire to come to Canada for the purpose of setting themselves up in business or to purchase farms. The availability of employment in various occupations and of small business or other opportunities, or the lack thereof, is forwarded regularly and frequently to immigration visa officers abroad to assist them in counselling prospective immigrants. The Department of Labour and the national employment service have been most co-operative in assisting this department in developing accurate information on employment conditions. Emphasis is placed on the sound counselling of prospective immigrants abroad in order that those who do come forward will be fully aware of what lies in store for them here.
It is confidently believed that economic conditions now warrant a more optimistic approach to immigration planning for 1959. As in 1958, unsponsored immigrants will be carefully selected according to their general suitability. They will be fully counselled as to employment and other conditions in Canada. Regardless of over-all economic conditions, there are always occupations and areas in Canada where immigrants can be placed, taking advantage of opportunities which the less mobile Canadian workers cannot or will not accept. As mentioned previously, immigration officers experienced little difficulty in finding employment for the unsponsored immigrants who came forward in 1958, and it is confidently anticipated that the same conditions will apply for 1959.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. lady has been very helpful in giving a very simple and factual statement on which we can base our observations about the immigration branch and its activities for the past year, and try to form some impression of what is likely to be the prospect for the year 1959. I must say that the hon. lady will perhaps be relieved to hear that I do not think she will find much quarrel on this side of the house with the position which is being taken by the government about open placement immigration. We might quarrel about things which are outside the hon. lady's control; that is to say, about the way in which this government has allowed the economy to deteriorate so that it is not safe for the hon. lady to encourage as many open placement

immigrants as we were able quite safely to encourage when we were in office, but that is another matter which I do not think it would be quite fair to discuss on the hon. lady's estimates.

You can talk about your

109.000	in 1955 or 1956.

The figures for 1956, as the hon. lady will perhaps remember, were I think the second highest since the war. No; there was one year earlier. But in any event, I am not particularly anxious to go into this past history, although I have no objection to doing so if the hon. lady wants a debate on that subject. I am much more concerned with talking about the situation which now exists and the prospective situation for 1959, because we obviously are not going to be able to do much about what has already happened. I do hope that the optimistic forecast which the hon. lady gave for 1959 will turn out to be right, because if I understood her correctly what she was saying was that conditions in Canada were going to be so bright before this year was over that she would be able to receive, without any difficulty so far as placement and settlement is concerned, a much larger number of immigrants than were received last year.
I must say that I doubt very much if this will be true, regardless of what improvement there may be in the economy, which we all hope for. Because one thing the hon. lady will I think learn when she has been a little longer in the department than she has been up to now is that there is a very serious time lag in immigration. When conditions become unfavourable for immigration and there is a discouragement of immigration, it takes quite a long time to get the steam up again. In 1955, after we had had a barrage all through the early months of that year from the hon. lady and other people who were on this side of the house about how the country was going to the dogs, because of unemployment, we found that had a very discouraging effect indeed upon immigration in that year. I am afraid that the figures of unemployment in this country, and certain recent incidents, will have that effect again.
One of the things that is going to be most discouraging to immigration prospects, particularly from the United Kingdom this year, is what happened last Friday, just one week ago. I, like most other hon. members, listened to or watched television, and I saw the workers coming out of the A. V. Roe plant,
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration many of them for the last time. As I listened to those voices, if my ear is any good, three out of four of them were English and obviously of relatively recent-I would say postwar-immigration. I am very much afraid that the blow to confidence that has been given there will result in a good many of these people going back home again. What is very likely to happen is that the Canadian born among these highly trained people, who are freely admitted to the United States, will go to the United States in numbers we will have cause to regret for many years. Those who are not Canadian born and therefore admissible to the United States only under quota will in many cases, particularly in the case of the British, tend to go home discouraged.
I cannot congratulate the hon. lady on one thing that happened in 1958 which had never happened before in the history of our postwar immigration. The hon. lady, presiding over this department in her first year, managed to get the British immigration into second place. Always in the past it had been in first place, and for a government which was going to do for the commonwealth that which we were said to have neglected to do, this is not a very proud record.
I have one other general criticism of the hon. lady's administration of the department. I do think that under her administration, so far as I have been able to observe it, the department has been unnecessarily restrictive in its attitude towards sponsored immigration. I repeat again that I have no criticism whatsoever to make of the open placement policy. I believe it would be very foolish to encourage people who have no ties with anybody in Canada to come here in the expectation of getting jobs only to find jobs very difficult to get.
I am not an immigration broker as the hon. lady well knows, but because I occupied for three years the position she now occupies I do have a certain number of these cases brought to my notice from time to time, and it does seem to me that there are a good many cases involving sponsored immigrants, or persons who are sought as sponsored immigrants, who have opportunities of employment or who, in some cases are not seeking employment, when permission to enter is denied in circumstances where entry would have no possible effect upon the labour market. It is true that they might in occasional cases come here to take a job with a relative which, had they not come, might conceivably have been offered to someone on the rolls of the national employment service, but in many more cases I would suspect that no one else would be employed at all.

I do think there is room for a little more flexibility and generosity, judging from a random sampling-and I confess it is no more-than appears to have been the practice during the past year, and particularly since parliament adjourned and since the new procedure which the hon. lady announced last August was adopted. I know what difficulties there are.
I do not think there is anyone in the house who knows better than I do what the difficulties with regard to these people are- people who come here claiming to be visitors but who really do not intend to be visitors at all but are just using the procedure as a back door method of getting into the country. I know what an embarrassment it can be, and I have recollections of being embarrassed in the house on some occasions about some of these cases. On the other hand it does seem to me that one of the things which a minister in charge of this department has to accept is a certain amount of embarrassment for doing what is intrinsically the right thing, even if it be sometimes misunderstood. However, I know of cases where there has, I think, been an unnecessary strictness with regard to visitors and an unnecessary amount of suspicion.
I do not intend to parade a lot of particular cases. As far as particular cases are concerned, I have always taken the view that the time of the committee should not be taken up with them unless a case is illustrative of some general principle, and when we come to deal with the citizenship branch it will not surprise the hon. lady if I tell her that I have a few cases of principle about which I intend to make some observations. But speaking generally, I will discuss with the department or with the hon. lady herself any individual cases I have in mind, and there are not many in which I am interested.
However, I want to make this general observation: I do think there is room, particularly if the hon. lady is really confident about the optimistic forecast she made, for a little more generosity and a little more relaxation, and perhaps a few more exceptions to the rigid application of the rules than has been applied to some of these cases in the last few months. I know how easy it is to become afraid of the economic situation, and with the mounting unemployment we have seen in the last few months I would not blame the hon. lady too much if she was frightened. But I do not think she frightens too easily, and I hope she will have the courage of the conviction she expressed this afternoon.

Don't worry about that.
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

I shall let the hon. lady do her own worrying. The hon. lady was not much given to criticizing the department over which she now presides when she was on this side of the house, but she has colleagues who were, and on this subject of sponsored immigration she will, of course, remember that there was a great deal of criticism of the administration of the department in former days, particularly in the last year during which I was minister. Possibly I should not make any reflection of even a general character, but I was about to say that perhaps that criticism was intended not so much to apply to the administration itself but was made with an eye on the effect it would have in headlines in the press. Anyway there was a good deal of criticism about the alleged heartless disregard shown by the department of the rights of Canadian citizens. I am not, of course, going to make any similar criticism, because I do not intend to change the position I took when I occupied the place now occupied by the hon. lady, and I must say that for this part of my observations I could wish that the Minister of Justice was here in her place, because he was one of the critics, and even when he was presiding only temporarily over the department he did say he had plans in progress to change the procedure.
I have always taken the view that nc person except a Canadian citizen and, to a limited extent, a landed immigrant who is temporarily out of the country has a right to enter Canada. The citizens of Canada, through parliament, have the right to decide who should be admitted and who should not be admitted and no rights of entry vest in individuals until those rights are acquired in Canada. However, this view was not taken by the present Minister of Justice or, so far as his somewhat obscure utterances seem to be capable of clear interpretation, by the Prime Minister. The Minister of Justice was clear about it, as he usually is, and he took the view that sponsors had some rights, that Canadian citizens have the rights to apply for relatives and that they have the right to have those applications considered in a judicial or quasi judicial manner. And the Minister of Justice when he was acting minister of this department did say something about this subject about a year ago on the estimates. I should like to remind the minister of what he said, because I should like to know whether she is pursuing this activity which the Minister of Justice said was being undertaken by the

present government to remove the iniquities of which we were supposed to be guilty when we were in office.
I asked the Minister of Justice on January 30, 1958 what was being done to deal with these cases where sponsors were being refused, and whether the reasons for refusal were going to be given-a procedure to which the Minister of Justice attached great importance. I do not wish to take up too much time with this. As reported at page 4058 of Hansard of January 30, I asked the following question:
Might I ask a question with respect to a term used by the minister. We all use the term "applicant" loosely: does the minister mean the sponsor or does he mean the immigrant?
The acting minister replied:
So far as getting authority for the revealing of information is concerned, it would have to be obtained from the proposed immigrant. The result of the studies we have been giving to this matter so far would indicate that if the information is released directly to the proposed immigrant, if he wishes to send it on to his proposed sponsor or to other interested parties, then that is up to him.
The word "reason" is used in that context with reference to the reason why someone was turned down. An unidentified hon. member then stated:
But they cannot get it.
The acting minister then went on to state:
The present policy and the past policy with regard to security cases is that information is not given, nothing is said. With regard to certain health cases, nothing is said. These are the problems with respect to which we have been giving a lot of study and which are under review at the present time.
I did not ask the hon. lady about this last August because I realized she had taken up this portfolio about the day the session began and I thought it would be unfair to expect her to have had time to familiarize herself with this admittedly intricate and difficult problem. That is why I did not bring it up then and I am bringing it up now when she has had many months in office during which to give attention to these matters. The acting minister of citizenship and immigration then went on to say:
Some of the work in my department has been subdivided so that certain committees can review the question of information in security cases, and with respect to immigration and citizenship, and information on rejections for health grounds.
I particularly draw the hon. lady's attention to the following words:
The system which I would like to see instituted and indeed the kind of system we have in mind, is a system where an applicant for admission to Canada or an applicant for the grant of a certificate of Canadian citizenship-perhaps I had better confine my remarks to immigration cases only for the moment-might be informed of the reasons for his

Citizenship and Immigration
rejection and might then have an opportunity to have his case reviewed by a board which would be guided by definite principles in considering that application so that the applicant or his sponsor in Canada-if he is sponsored-may if he wishes present his case to a review panel, and so that he will know and have a hearing.
I may say that I do not personally advocate what the hon. gentleman was then advocating. I do not advocate it because I do not believe it is practical or practicable. When the hon. gentleman and the hon. lady were on this side of the chamber they made a terrific indictment of the former administration because it failed to do these things. The present Minister of Justice a year ago told us that the department was giving active study to this matter and was trying to work out procedures for dealing with these cases. I would be exceedingly interested if, when the hon. lady replies, she would tell us whether these ideas have now been given up, whether the government has come to the conclusion that after all we were right-as I think we were-or whether it intends to take these matters out of the immigration branch and hand them over to quasi judicial boards of some description or other to give reasons where applications from sponsors are refused or what the procedure is to be.
This is an extremely important matter indeed. It was the contention of the Minister of Justice, not merely when he sat in this side of the chamber but even a year ago, when he was sitting over there, that these sponsors have certain rights. In view of the legislative menu for this session, with the bill of rights as the main course, it seems to me this is one thing we should clear up finally one way or the other on these estimates. We should know if the government takes the position taken by the Minister of Justice.
My own view is that the proper attitude is the one taken by almost every other country in the world under which parliament- if there is a parliament in the country-has control of the entry and that no right should inhere in persons who are not citizens of that country. Even in the declaration of human rights of the United Nations the right of migration from one country to another has never been included and so far as I know it has never been suggested for inclusion.
I do not wish to appear to take a heartless view. I am a strong believer in sponsored immigration. I believe it is by far the best kind of immigration. The reason for that is that the sponsored immigrant comes to someone he knows or who is related to him with, so to speak, a certain connection with the country before he arrives and there is perhaps at least a 50 per cent greater chance on

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the average that he will orient himself to his new surroundings more easily and satisfactorily. Of course, you can have open applicant immigrants who turn out to be quite remarkable people and sponsored ones who turn out to be egregious failures. We all appreciate that. However, I do not think I would find any quarrel in the committee with the view that, on the average, sponsored immigration is on balance much more likely to be successful and capable of being carried on with less dislocation to the country and to the individuals than open placement migration. I believe I have already said that I thought the hon. lady was a little too tough in her treatment of sponsored cases. That is the impression I have. That is one thing. It is another thing to say we are going to establish a system of rights in this field with judicial or quasi judicial boards to determine what those rights are. I think the government and the minister should now be in a position to tell us what the government's intentions really are in this matter.
I do not intend to take the whole time of the committee until five o'clock but there are one or two other questions I should like to put now though I will not elaborate on them. I will merely state my questions so that the hon. lady may have an opportunity to have them looked up for the next time we come before the committee.
The minister will recall that shortly before I left the department we undertook some special procedures for the admission of limited categories of persons from Poland once it became apparent that, because of the political evolution there, it was possible for some people to get out. I should be very interested as I am sure all hon. members of the committee would be, to have a report on how that has worked, how it is working now and approximately how many people have been involved.
Now that the West Indies Federation has been formed-and the hon. lady of course has visited it-I have been wondering what views the government has about the question of immigration from the West Indies and in order that the hon. lady will not have to ask me what my views are I shall state them right now. If I had remained in office I had intended to suggest to my colleagues that once the federation was formed we should seek to negotiate a quota system similar to what we have with India, Pakistan and Ceylon. I am not wedded to that particular view and perhaps the government has better ideas but I believe there is a problem here that simply cannot be glossed over, a problem that I confess was a good deal of worry to me.
I should also like to know what the situation is in Hong Kong and whether we are finally disposing of that problem which should be disposed of largely by the passage of time.
I would be particularly interested if the hon. lady could bring us up to date on the Hungarian settlement situation. She gave us figures last year which were very encouraging at least to me when she told us that only about 500 of the 35,000 had gone home, and I think we were well rid of those 500. At that time which, of course was last August, there were about 500 others actually receiving help from the department which indicated that the vast majority of them had at least got themselves settled to some degree. I think this is quite remarkable, considering that these people came here with nothing whatever, unlike practically any other group of immigrants we have ever had. In that context-and here again I am not seeking to be in the slightest degree controversial-I should like to say to the hon. lady that I understand the government has before it an application from the University of British Columbia for some further limited assistance in order to complete the education of the Hungarian students in the forestry faculty there. I understand that an application is before the government for this purpose and I want to assure the hon. lady that she will find no dissent in our party if she accedes to that request.
I should like in one word to give my reasons for taking this view. Bringing this whole faculty from behind the iron curtain to Canada, was one of the things that caught the imagination of the free world at the time it was done. Whatever the situation inside Canada may be, the international effect of having that experiment fail and having it said behind the iron curtain that we were not able to handle this problem would, I think, be very damaging not merely to the reputation of Canada but to the reputation of the free world. It is unfortunate that 1957 and 1958 were both poor years in the forest industry of British Columbia or this problem would not have arisen. For that reason I think there would be very strong grounds which would commend themselves to most sensible men and women for acceding to the very modest request, as I understand it, of the University of British Columbia. I do not wish to continue now but I may wish to make some other brief observations or ask questions later on.
You may carry on for another five minutes.
I do not think I have five minutes more.
We will give it to you.
I hoped the hon. member for Vancouver East was going to follow me.
I would love to, but not for five minutes.
If he does not wish to follow for five minutes, there are one or two other things I would like to ask about.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-8, to provide for minimum wages for employees.

He said: In introducing this bill, I think it would be wise to refer to the explanatory notes which are very simple and which read as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a minimum rate of wages with respect to all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. This bill provides that such minimum rate of wages shall be $1.25 per hour. The bill also provides that its terms do not affect any employee whose rate of wages is higher than the minimum established by this legislation. However, any rate of wages less favourable to employees than $1.25 per hour is superseded by this bill.
It has been generally recognized by this government and the former government that there is a need in Canada for the establishment of a federal labour code. This bill, if passed, would provide one part of a federal labour code. In addition to this bill, we have now under the Department of Labour the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and if a federal labour code were introduced we would add such measures as an annual vacations with pay act; statutory holidays with pay act; maximum hours of work act and other acts of a similar nature affecting labour under the jurisdiction of the federal government. This bill is not new, as it was introduced into this house in 1957.
The first time a minimum wage bill was discussed in this house was in 1935 under the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. At that time, Mr. Bennett, a former Conservative leader, introduced legislation to implement part of the recommendations of the 1928 Geneva conference because Canada was a signatory to the convention that followed. In 1928, the League of Nations set up an international labour office in Geneva, and during the eleventh session of the international labour conference certain recommendations were made which would be binding on those nations that signed the convention. One recommendation was that this convenion be implemented by the countries that signed it.
If we refer to the report of the proceedings of this international labour conference we find that at page 624 they discussed a minimum wage act. These are the directions given to the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett by the international labour organization when he tried to pass his minimum wage act. Section II reads:
For the purpose of determining the minimum rates of wages to be fixed the wage fixing body should in any case take account of the necessity of enabling the workers concerned to maintain a suitable standard of living. For this purpose regard should primarily be had to the rates of wages being paid for similar work in trades where the workers are adequately organized and have concluded effective collective agreements or, if no such standard of reference is available in the

circumstances, to the general level of wages prevailing in the country or in the particular locality.
For effectively protecting the wages of the workers concerned and safeguarding the employers affected against the possibility of unfair competition, the measures to be taken to ensure that wages are not paid at less than the minimum rates which have been fixed are to include:
(1)	arrangements for informing the employers and workers of the rates in force;
(2)	official supervision of the rates actually being paid: and
(3)	sanctions for remedying and preventing infringements of the rates in force.
The Conservative government of that day believed that this was fair and just and, having signed the convention, proceeded to introduce a measure to implement it in Canada. The resultant act is to be found in the statutes of Canada, chapter 44, 1935. When introducing this matter the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was concerned about the effect it would possibly have and some of the objections that might be taken because of the British North America Act. For these reasons he outlined in the preamble many conditions that he hoped would make this measure acceptable to the Canadian people. However, governments being what they are, his government was defeated and a Liberal government followed under the Right Hon. Mackenzie King who referred the matter to the supreme court where it was held the act was ultra vires of the federal government.
The matter of a minimum wage law for Canadians was discussed in the house on a number of occasions in the intervening years until 1957, at which time Mr. Stanley Knowles, who had supported this idea for many years, introduced a bill similar to the one I am now introducing. I have had to change the rate in this bill to bring it into line with the standard of living, as was suggested by the Geneva conference. I think it is necessary, because of the geographical conditions prevailing in Canada and also because of the British North America Act which
Industrial Relations
places some of the rights of labour under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments and some under the federal government, to take a look at what has happened in this field over the intervening years in the various provinces.
In every case, with the exception of Prince Edward Island, there are now on the statute books of the provinces various forms of minimum wage legislation. These pieces of legislation have been amended from time to time so that in many conditions they are not similar to one another, although in general they are. By 1958, the British Columbia act had been revised so that the minimum wage rate was set at 65 cents an hour instead of the previous weekly rate of $22 per week or 55 cents an hour. The Manitoba act was amended in 1957 to produce a rate of 60 cents an hour for males and increase the rate for women by two and three cents an hour. In Saskatchewan. the minimum was raised in 1957 from $26 to $30 per week in the towns, and from $24.50 to $29 in the larger cities. In Quebec the minimum rate was revised in 1957 to 60 cents an hour in zone 1, 55 cents in zone 2, and 50 cents in zone 3, an increase in each case of nine cents an hour. New Brunswick increased the rate from 38 to 45 cents an hour for women in hotels and restaurants and from 40 to 50 cents an hour in other types of employment. Nova Scotia also set new rates of $21.60 a week in zone 1, other rates applying in other zones.
As we can see by these rates, there is a great variance in the minimum rates across the country. With the permission of the house I should like to put on Hansard pages 12 and 13 of a Department of Labour publication containing charts of the minimum rates in effect in the various provinces.

Because of the suggestions that have been made at various times I think it is only fair that we should ask for minimum rates set higher than the average rates in Canada. To take a look at some of the rates, I think we should start with some of the lower ones in such industries as the canned and preserved fruits and vegetables industry. This information is reported in a pamphlet put out by "The Honourable Gordon Churchill, Minister of Trade and Commerce" and is entitled "Man-Hours and Hourly Earnings with Average Weekly Wages, December, 1958". In the canned and preserved fruits and vegetables industry the average hourly earnings as of December 1, 1958 in cents, was 113.7; in the leather products industry, 114.8; boots and shoes, 109.3. In each case the number of people working in the industry was less than 20,000. In service industries, for hotels and restaurants, the average was 96.7 cents an hour, with 34,000 employees; for laundries and dry cleaning plants, with the lowest average of all industries in Canada, the average was 97.3 cents, with only 14,750 employees.
But the large bulk of the employed persons in Canada that are reporting to the dominion bureau of statistics-805,117 employees in manufacturing-earn an average of 167.2 cents. In some industries like mining, with 75,545 employees, they earn 197.9 cents per hour. From these figures-and we could mention others that are exceptionally high like primary iron and steel at 229.3 per hour for 28,000 people-it can be seen that in asking for $1.25 an hour we are certainly not asking for an exorbitant amount of money.
We should like this minimum wage law to be put into effect and be incorporated in a Canadian labour code. This code has been asked for by the Canadian Labour Congress. It has been asked for by the C.C.C.L. It has been asked for by many of the national unions. I think it is desired by all employees in Canada. I am happy to say that the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has asked the various labour organizations for suggestions as to what the labour organizations would wish established in a federal labour code. I commend the Minister of Labour for his initiative. In view of his record in these matters, and certainly in following that of the former leader of the Conservative party, R. B. Bennett, I think we can expect to see something done in this line in the very near future. We are asking for a federal code but we are also asking in this bill for this provision to be applied only to those employees under federal jurisdiction. These are few in number. They take in such

employees as those in banks, in communications, in transportation, in civil service and a few other various industries.
Then I would point out that this minimum wage of $1.25 is not to be considered as a wage but is to be considered as a minimum wage and all other wages should seek to be higher. One of the advantages of having the federal government pass this type of legislation is that it sets a pattern for the provincial governments to follow. I think that this pattern is something that is desirable. Certainly the need for this type of legislation has been pointed out in the province of Newfoundland where conditions are certainly not as would be suggested if we had a Canadian federal labour code.
The federal government by passing this type of legislation is going to raise the standard of living of very few people because the majority of people under federal jurisdiction are now receiving a much higher rate of pay than this. But it will set for the provincial governments a pattern at which they can aim and by which they can hope to raise the standards in each of the provinces. This procedure is necessitated by the fact that the British North America Act made a division between those jurisdictions that come under the federal code and those that would not be covered under a federal code. The rate of $1.25 is the amount that has been asked for by the Canadian Labour Congress when they came to the government a few months ago, on January 22 of this year. In making their presentation, they had this to say:
We believe parliament should enact a national minimum wage of $1.25 an hour and a national maximum work-week of 40 hours.
Certainly this last would be happily received in the province of Newfoundland. Then they go on to say this:
In our last appearance before you we suggested to you that you might try to convene a conference with the provinces with a view to establishing uniform nationwide legislation on labour relations. We set out in some detail what we thought such a conference might accomplish. We also suggested to you, as we have suggested in our proposed amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, that industries of nation-wide scope and importance should be brought under the act as has been done with grain elevators, for example.
In asking for this minimum of $1.25, which is 25 cents higher than was asked for by Mr. Stanley Knowles when he introduced this bill or a similar one in 1957, we are taking into consideration the inflationary trend and the need for an increased wage to keep up with the standard of living. In asking for the passing of this act we are also asking that favourable consideration be given to maintaining equal pay for equal work so

that women as well as men will be able to obtain the benefits of a minimum wage of $1.25.
I think there may be some objection in some parts of Canada to a rate of $1.25 because this is an arbitrary figure. It may be higher in some provinces in relation to the average rate of pay in that province than it will be in others. In the passing of this bill I think some consideration can be given to geographical locations and the rates of pay in various localities. This is something that can be done when and if this bill is referred to the standing committee on industrial relations. This bill could be amended so that it would take into consideration some of these geographical factors. I think consideration should be given by the house at this time to the passing of this minimum wage act so that we can give leadership to the provinces of Canada and can comply with the wishes expressed and the conventions entered into at the international labour conference long ago in 1928.

Mr. Speaker, before taking part in this debate I would like to check whether the actual bill is in order in that clause 4 states $1 an hour, whereas the explanation states $1.25 an hour.
I imagine it is a typographical error which the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has had changed in the house. If that is so, then I would like to go back to November 28, 1957, when Mr. Knowles first introduced his bill, because with the exception of the change from $1 to $1.25, and a rather minor change in the rates to be deducted for board and room, this bill is identical with the bill introduced by Mr. Knowles.
Mr. Knowles, in the same manner as the hon. member for Timiskaming, went back to 1935 when the government of Mr. Bennett, who was prime minister at that time, presented to parliament what was popularly known as the Bennett new deal legislation. Mr. Knowles went on to say that in this new deal legislation was incorporated a minimum wages act; but this was found to be ultra vires of the federal parliament and was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada by the Liberal government which came into office after the election in 1935. The reason it was declared ultra vires is that the court plainly stated that labour matters come in part only under federal jurisdiction, and part under provincial jurisdiction. Therefore it was not proper for the federal government to enact the legislation proposed by Mr. Bennett.
Industrial Relations
Mr. Knowles then got around that point in his bill by limiting its application to employees who come under federal jurisdiction. At the same time he made reference to the brief, as did the hon. member for Timiskaming, which was presented by the Canadian Labour Congress on October 21, 1957, in which Mr. Jodoin stated as follows. I am now quoting from page 1620 of Hansard for November 28, 1957:
But the dominion should not confine itself to doing as well as the best of the provinces.
He is referring to the $1 minimum wage proposed in Mr. Knowles' bill.
It should give a lead. It should, specifically, establish a legal maximum work week of 40 hours and a legal maximum wage of $1 an hour. This is not really a very drastic proposal.
Later on he goes on to say that a minimum of $1 an hour might be hard to apply immediately, but in most provinces the legal minimum rates are preposterously low. Mr. Jodoin did recognize that there would be difficulties in the application of this type of legislation, and that it would take some time. I find it rather strange that the hon. member for Timiskaming should feel that in the short space of a year or slightly more the rather difficult proposition of selling this to the provinces could be made easier by a general increase of 25 per cent, raising it from $1 to $1.25.
There was reference made in regard to comparison with United States figures and United States legislation. The legislation in the United States is called the fair labour standards act. This act was enacted by the United States congress in 1948 and it established a national minimum rate of pay and a maximum work week in industries under United States federal jurisdiction. The act initially set a minimum wage objective of 40 cents per hour which was to be reached in successive stages over a period of seven years. Subsequent amendments increased the minimum wage from 40 cents to 75 cents per hour in 1950, and to the present minimum of $1 an hour in 1956. But in the United States, because of their control of interstate commerce there are some 24 million workers who come under federal control.
In Canada there are only about 400,000 employees in industries which are under federal jurisdiction. Now, of those 400,000 employees some 70 per cent, or 280,000, come under collective bargaining agreements, which the hon. member will admit is the proper and best way to set wages. Of the remainder who are not covered under collective bargaining agreements, a very small percentage will have wages lower than $1 an hour. The figures given by the labour department indicate there

Industrial Relations
are some 20,000 lower than $1 an hour, and in the case of $1.25 I would estimate it would not be materially higher because the classifications covered by federal legislation are not usually the lowest paid people in the country. There is no doubt that minimum wages acts have a very fine purpose, and that is to see that the worker gets a living wage. But other factors have to be borne in mind. The capacity of industry to pay, the nature of the work and service, and the general level of wages.
In this same debate to which I referred on November 28, 1957, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) pointed out that the minimum basic rates established by provincial legislation varied considerably, and I am indeed grateful to the hon. member for Timiskaming for putting on record a factual statement in regard to these various rates. The method of setting minimum wage rates in the provinces does vary from the method proposed in this bill in that they are usually handled by minimum wage boards who have the power to adjust these wages by regulation. A weakness in this bill is that you have to come to parliament every time you want an adjustment, and the hon. member has shown that in the short space of one year he considers the adjustment should have been 25 per cent above that proposed previously by the very able spokesman of his party. So that means that if this kept on it would be a yearly matter. However, the way the provinces operate is to set up a minimum wage board which has the power, through regulation, to set minimum rates. This bill therefore embodies a new approach in Canada as far as setting a minimum wage is concerned.
In regard to minimum rates in the provinces at the present time, some of these, as the hon. member has said, are quite low. He did point out, I believe, that they varied from some 35 cents to 75 cents an hour. He pointed out a zoning system was used in certain provinces; in other provinces there is a differential between urban and city areas. The hon. member's bill would, I think, try to make the federal government beat a club over the heads of the provinces by invading their field. From the figures I have given and the admissions of the hon. member himself, there is no real need for this measure as far as employees coming under federal jurisdiction are concerned. These are not the people he is aiming at. He is aiming at those areas under provincial control which do not at the present time have a wage level equivalent to what he is proposing, and he did read out certain figures from the Department of Trade and Commerce to bear out his contention.

I think it is not a good thing for this parliament deliberately to invade the fields which are set apart for the provinces, especially as all the provinces except one-Prince Edward Island-do have minimum wage boards or other means of setting minimum wages.
This minimum may appear low by our standards, and when I say "our standards"
I am thinking of the province of British Columbia from which I come. However, it must be remembered that there are many varying factors to be taken into account. The range of occupations covered must necessarily be large, including farm labourers, domestic servants and baby sitters and other groups not yet represented by labour organizations. In addition, the place of work also varies widely from urban areas to remote rural areas.
I think the proper way to set wages is by collective bargaining and mutual agreement between employers and employees. To try to do it by setting a minimum wage level which would have a blanket application throughout the country is in my opinion misguided. It would be unenforcible because it is a matter outside our jurisdiction, and in any case it would be almost unenforcible in practice.
The point which the hon. member made with regard to such a bill setting a pattern for the provinces does not appear to me to have much validity, because I think the provinces will continue to do just what they think is in the best interests of their people and in the best interests of the development of industry. There may be one exception to that. Although no one can quarrel with the intent of the bill, which is to try to provide better wages for the workers of Canada, I believe there are much better ways in which the objective which the hon. member has in mind could be accomplished.
At the heart of the bill lies, as I have said, this figure of $1.25 an hour, if we leave out the question of board and lodging. I do not understand why that matter was ever put into the measure because, as the hon. member knows, construction workers and others engaged in employments which require them to work away from home and where special provision is required for board and lodging are almost invariably covered by union agreements, with the exception, perhaps, of domestic servants and farm labourers.
I think the hon. member will be disappointed if he hopes that in some of the agricultural provinces the farmers are going to look with much favour on this proposition, or if he thinks that the agricultural provinces which would have control over this field would pass any such measure. The best way to

settle the wages of farm labourers is by agreement between employer and employee, with the scarcity of farm labour giving the employee his greatest bargaining strength. It is, of course, admittedly more difficult for this kind of labour to be adequately represented through collective bargaining.
In conclusion I would draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that ability to pay must also be part of any wage settlement. So although in principle we support the idea of trying to do what the hon. member wishes to do, and although we hope that the provinces will continue as they have done in the past making provision by regulation for continual increase in minimum wages to keep in step with the times, this bill is certainly not the way in which it should be done.

In rising at this time to take a small part in the debate I wish to assure the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) that I appreciate his sincerity in bringing in a bill of this kind which in many ways could benefit those who have to work for a living. Most of us I am sure would agree in principle with most parts of the bill. Nevertheless, I consider that I must point out some of the problems we should face if we were to embark on legislation of this kind at the present time.
I have had considerable experience of labour legislation and I was for many years a member of a labour organization. I have acted on arbitration boards, on bargaining committees, and on a great many other committees dealing with labour. This bill, in my view, is one that should be considered from a regional standpoint. I do not think we could justly set up a minimum wage which would be fair and equal in all parts of Canada. I do not feel, for example, that I am in a position to say that a $1.25 an hour would be a fair minimum wage in and around the Toronto area or, to go to extremes, in the northern parts of Ontario, Quebec and Newfoundland. I do not feel, therefore, that it would be possible at the present time to put into effect, and make workable, a minimum wage which would be fair in all parts of Canada unless this were done on a regional basis.
We must all remember that in the provinces we have departments of labour and ministers of labour and that it is their job to provide good legislation suitable to the provinces which they serve. I do not think that we in Ottawa should try to invade their field, at least at the present time. I said that I have had some experience in labour matters, and I should like to refer to the industrial standards act which is an act to provide for minimum wages and
Industrial Relations
reasonable hours of work. That act has been on the statute books in the province of Ontario for some 15 years and throughout those years they have never been able to put it into effect in such a way as to make it work.
I may say that I have had some experience with that on an enforcing committee. It was not the employers of labour who gave us the greater problem. It was the employees themselves. If you set a minimum wage rate that is more than the prevailing rate in an area you immediately have a problem. After all, this is a free country and if a man chooses to work for $1 an hour it is going to be a big responsibility for someone to make him work for $1.25 an hour. A problem of enforcement is created. Who is going to enforce legislation of that kind? Who can make it work? Is it going to be done by the local municipal police, the provincial police or the R.C.M.P.? If you place an act on the statute books and want to make it effective it has to be enforced. The problem of enforcing a minimum wage entails a great deal of expense and a large number of persons who could serve to enforce it.
I feel that we should be cautious before proceeding to pass a law that is going to affect the whole of Canada. I made some reference to putting such a provision into effect. In communities where there is a minimum wage and where that wage is perhaps higher than the prevailing rate you find it has a tendency to pull down the prevailing rate to the minimum. There is no mistake about that. When contractors go into an area to tender on jobs they will tender at the rate set by the government, the minimum rate. Again a problem arises. If the minimum rate is higher than the prevailing rate it creates a disturbance in the area and problems arise that have to be met. Before we go too far with respect to a measure of this kind I feel we should give serious consideration to the point I have mentioned.
The riding that I represent is one of the most highly unionized in the whole of Canada but as I stand here and say that I do not feel I am not a friend of labour. I know that as far as our community is concerned minimum wages are not considered to be too important as a subject of labour legislation. There was a time in the years gone by before unions became as widespread and well organized as they are today-and I might say I participated to a considerable extent in the organization of at least one- when perhaps the need for a minimum wage was greater than at present but unions across the country are doing an excellent job in preventing what we used to refer to as slave labour. Between the unions and the

Industrial Relations
provincial departments of labour the situation is being pretty well taken care of at this time. I suggest that we proceed with extreme caution in respect of this question because it could lead us into a serious problem involving enforcement and result in unfairness across Canada that we do not wish to see. I know there are others who wish to speak to this matter so with those remarks I shall conclude.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, this bill, in so far as it is designed to improve the lot of the working classes in Canada, should no doubt be welcomed by hon. members. However, I fail to see how, in its present form, it can help achieve the purpose contemplated by its mover.
In the first place, as I already said, it applies only to a very small category of employees, those under the federal government jurisdiction, about 400,000 in number. Now, more than half and perhaps even two-thirds or three-quarters of those 400,000 employees, are under various collective bargaining agreements. As for the others, they are mostly casual workers paid at prevailing rates.
Therefore, as regards employees directly covered by this bill, this legislation would offer them no substantial improvement, since their working conditions are already fairly good, if not better than those proposed.
It has been said that this legislation could serve as a model for the other provinces. How can anyone make such a claim, when nine of ten provinces have already adopted adequate minimum salary legislations for the particular conditions of their area. So much for the purpose of the bill.
Then again, the way it is worded, I do not think its application would be very practical. As a matter of fact, one of the employers-and the employer, in this case, will be either the government, the corporations, or the agencies or commissions coming under them-would have to pay a minimum of $1 an hour to all its employees; I even believe that it is $1.25, although, as I have already pointed out, the bill itself refers in section 4 to $1 an hour. Therefore, any time economic conditions changed, we would have to amend the bill or have it amended by parliament. Furthermore, there is no distinction being made between employees who could be paid not only by the hour, but also by the week,

by the month, by the year, by contract or by the job. There is no provision for such cases. The case of apprentices is not provided for either. Apprentices, that is those who are in training, are not getting that minimum salary of $1.25 an hour.
Nor is any distinction made between Canada's various economic regions. It has been said time and again in this house-I believe it is a well-known fact-that Canada is a federation of various regions each with its particular economic problems and that, therefore, wage levels fluctuate tremendously between provinces. For instance, Mr. Speaker, you need only refer to the minimum wage act of the province of Quebec. The provincial minimum wage board has had to establish three regions or areas with varying wage levels. So if it is necessary in one province to make a distinction between wage levels in different areas, it is even more so in a vast country such as this, where economic conditions, according to all economists in the country and all people, differ widely. Of course, a minimum wage applied, for instance, in cities with a metropolitan area, like Toronto and Montreal, could not be applicable in remote rural areas.
Moreover, no consideration has been given to the good of the industry itself. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), who introduced this bill, quoted certain figures showing that salaries are higher in some industries than in others. There is a very obvious reason for this difference which, in my view does not imply unfairness. On the contrary, it is a practical application of the principle of different pay for different work. In some industries, there are light jobs that can easily be performed by students, by youths or even by part time women workers. By using such labour, those industries are able to produce goods and sell them at a reasonable price allowing for a profit.
Subjecting all those industries to a standard rate of salary higher than present salaries would place them in a position where they could no longer compete with other similar industries in Canada and, perhaps more important, with other industries abroad. What would happen then? Surely there would be another unemployment crisis, because such action would restrict Canada's economic activity.
For all those reasons, I feel that this bill is not appropriate. In my view, parliament should not legislate or enact laws that cannot

be enforced because of the constitutional problems involved and also because of present economic conditions.
However, if I may be allowed to put forward a proposal in connection with minimum wages, I would suggest not in the form of an amendment, but merely as a suggestion- that legislation be passed to make it possible to enforce the minimum wage provisions that are now in the statute books in nine of the ten provinces with regard to employees under federal jurisdiction. This would take into account the variety of economic factors across the country, and at the same time, it would assert the principle that apparently the hon. member for Timiskaming has in mind, namely that every man's labour should receive a fair and equitable reward and that the federal government should give leadership in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I see by the clock there are only two minutes left. I should like to agree with most of those who have gone before me in approving the principle of this bill, but I find that a practical application of that principle would be another matter.
Much mention has been made of the Bennett legislation of 1935. Of course, there is a vast difference between that legislation and what we have before us today in the fact that that legislation applied not only to the people under federal jurisdiction but to all employees of the country. When we look back to the supreme court decision which was given at that time we find it interesting to note that the legislation was rejected by only three judges to two. It might be well to have another look to see if it would not be within the competence of the federal government to undertake such

I would note that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) pointed out that one of the reasons why the Bennett legislation was passed was to provide for the ratifying of the convention of the international labour organization.
